extracted.intended_audience: European patent attorneys, applicants, EPO examiners and other IP practitioners interested in EPO prosecution practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-law standards governing when and how the description of a European patent application must be amended to conform with the claims, including relevant EPO Guidelines provisions, EPC articles/rules, and Board of Appeal decisions. Focused on the legal basis for deleting claim-like or redundant/contradictory subject-matter from the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO Guidelines requirement to amend description in line with the claims (H‑V 2.7; F‑IV 4.3(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO Guidelines for Examination require applicants to amend the description of a European patent application in line with the scope of the allowable claims (H‑V, 2.7 and F‑IV, 4.3(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the current Guidelines applicants are required either to delete subject matter no longer covered by the claims or explicitly state that the offending subject matter does not fall under the scope of the invention. The post notes this requirement has become 'rather draconian' in recent years and that examiners continue to require conformity with these Guidelines despite conflicting Board of Appeal decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 84 EPC — claims must be clear, concise and supported by the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 84 EPC stipulates that the claims 'shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.' It is often cited as legal support for requiring description amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Boards/Examiners rely on Article 84 to require deletion or amendment of description passages; however, decisions such as T 1989/18 and T 1444/20 have held that Article 84 cannot justify removing description matter where the claims are clear in and of themselves without recourse to the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: F‑IV.4.4 — deletion/amendment of claim-like clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidelines state 'claim-like clauses must also be deleted or amended to avoid claim-like language prior to grant since they otherwise may lead to unclarity on the subject-matter for which protection is sought' (F‑IV.4.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board in T 1444/20 found that if the claims of the main request are clear without reference to the description, the mere presence of claim-like clauses in the description that are not part of the claims cannot affect clarity; therefore deletion may not be warranted. The Guidelines' categorical requirement to always remove such clauses was criticised as inconsistent with that reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 42(1)(c) EPC — description must disclose the invention as claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 42(1)(c) EPC requires that the description must disclose the invention as claimed in such terms that the technical problem and its solution can be understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board in T 1444/20 did not accept that this provision translates into a requirement to remove passages of the description that disclose embodiments which are not claimed, particularly where the technical problem solved by the claims can be clearly understood from the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 48(1)(c) EPC — no obviously irrelevant or unnecessary subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 48(1)(c) EPC stipulates that a European patent application should not contain obviously irrelevant or unnecessary subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a number of Boards have relied on Rule 48(1)(c) as a legal basis for requiring the description to be adapted to the subject-matter as claimed, T 1989/18 and T 1444/20 rejected using Rule 48 as justification for refusing grant merely because the description contains 'unnecessary' matter. The post quotes reasoning that it would be 'perverse' to refuse grant for such reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity test — are claims clear in and of themselves without reference to the description?
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical test applied by Boards: determine whether the claims are clear in and of themselves (i.e., without needing recourse to the description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are clear on their own, the presence of claim-like or redundant passages in the description that are not part of the claims cannot affect claim clarity, and deletion of such passages may be unnecessary. T 1989/18 and T 1444/20 support this principle; it directly contradicts a blanket application of the Guidelines' amendment requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deletion warranted only where description passages cause lack of clarity or contradiction with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Description passages should be deleted or amended when they give rise to unclarity about the subject-matter for which protection is sought, or when they are contradictory to the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: T 1444/20 emphasises that deletion is not justified merely because content is 'redundant' or not claimed; deletion is more defensible where the description causes lack of clarity or contains subject-matter inconsistent with the claims. Boards have differed on whether and when such contradictions require deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish redundant versus contradictory subject-matter when assessing need for amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a legal and practical distinction between redundant (unclaimed but not conflicting) and contradictory (inconsistent with the claims) subject-matter in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: T 1444/20 concerned deletion of redundant subject-matter and found deletion unnecessary where claims remain clear; by contrast T 1989/18 and T 1024/18 relate to contradictory subject-matter. This distinction affects whether Rule 42/48 or Article 84 can be used to justify amendment or deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical weight of Board of Appeal decisions — distribution codes and persuasive value
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution code attached to Board decisions (e.g., 'C' vs 'D') affects whether a decision is distributed to other Boards and thus its visibility and persuasive impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions with a 'D' distribution code (e.g., T 1444/20 and T 1989/18) may not be circulated to other Boards, reducing their practical influence on examiner practice, whereas 'C' coded decisions (e.g., T 1024/18, T 2766/17, T 2293/18) have been distributed and used to support the Guidelines' approach. Practitioners should be mindful that examiners may continue to follow the Guidelines irrespective of isolated Board decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When conflicting case-law exists, consider referral to the Enlarged Board of Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: If Boards of Appeal produce clearly divergent case law on a legal issue (here, description amendments), the matter may warrant a referral to the Enlarged Board for authoritative resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post suggests that the growing number of conflicting decisions on description amendments makes it increasingly likely that a referral to the Enlarged Board of Appeal will be required to resolve the legal uncertainty; practitioners facing inconsistent examiner requests may consider procedural routes to obtain clarity.
